newsitem.title: USA: Accounting board wants derivatives plan by June 97.
newsitem.headline: Accounting board wants derivatives plan by June 97.

text.p: The Financial Accounting Standards Board hopes to complete its four-year project to overhaul accounting rules for derivatives by June 1997, despite heavy criticism of its latest proposal.

"Almost anything that we could think of in this area would be controversial to at least some parties," chairman Dennis Beresford said Friday. "This latest proposal is, at least, less controversial than some of the earlier versions."
Beresford said the board would revisit every issue in the current proposal but still hoped to finish its work by next June.

"Our plan still is to issue the final document by June 30, 1997 although the timing and contents obviously depend greatly on what changes we make based on the input we received," Beresford said in a speech at a conference of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants conference.
"We're going to very carefully consider all of the suggestions and see if there is a way of improving our document," Beresford said.
So far, most feedback has been negative. Of 254 comment letters sent to the board on the proposal, only two wholeheartedly endorsed the draft, he said.
The board will hold public hearings starting next week. Representatives of 40 companies and organizations have asked to testify, Beresford said.
Fundamentally, the board aims to require companies to carry all derivatives, on their balance sheets at current market values.

Under current practice, many derivatives -- financial instruments whose value is based on the value of another instrument, asset or market index -- are carried off-balance sheet, and similiar transactions may receive disparate accounting treatment.
However, most of the controversy stems from the board's proposed treatment of changes in the value of derivatives once they are carried on balance sheets.
In some cases, companies would have to include the changes in value in their net income. Some comment letters complained that would create misleading earnings volatility.

If a derivative was used to hedge another asset or liability, the company could offset changes in value of the derivative with changes in value of the hedged item. But use of so-called hedge accounting would be strictly limited -- too much so, according to some commentators.
The accounting board will consider, as some comment letters suggested, creating a special category for companies that use only simple derivatives as part of their debt management, Beresford said.

"We will consider it again, but I really don't know where we'll come down," Beresford said. Use of the same instruments on a larger scale could create complications for such a special category, he said.

In the past, the board proposed forcing companies to carry all financial instruments -- not just derivatives -- at current market values. Corporations bashed the proposal and the board backed off. But it remains a future goal, "five to 10 years away," Beresford said. --Aaron Pressman, 202-898-8312
